title: The world is burning (146–150)
hookLine: why laughter, why joy, when the world is always burning; this body a city built of bones

lines: A PHOTO FROM TEN YEARS AGO.
cards: Look at a photo of yourself from ten years ago. Maybe you laugh at the haircut. Maybe you feel a small pang.
The face is you and not quite you. Something has been quietly happening the whole time, day and night, and it hasn't paused once.

Chapter eleven of the Dhammapada is called old age, and its first line sounds almost rude, like someone walking into a party and asking why everyone's laughing. It isn't meant as gloom. It's meant as a wake-up.

teach.h: WHY LAUGHTER, IF THE WORLD BURNS?
teach.b: Verse one forty-six, in Max Müller's translation: "How is there laughter, how is there joy, as this world is always burning? Why do you not seek a light, ye who are surrounded by darkness?"
The Buddha uses burning elsewhere too.

teach.h: THE FIRE SERMON: ALL IS BURNING.
teach.b: In a discourse known as the fire sermon, he tells a thousand monks, once fire-worshippers, that everything is burning: the eye, the ear, the mind, all burning with the fires of greed, hatred and delusion, and with birth, aging and death.
If the house is on fire, why keep partying in it? And the verse doesn't say despair. It says: seek a light.
The next verses look straight at the body. The old commentary sets verse one forty-seven beside a story. Sirimā, a well-known and beautiful courtesan in the city of Rajagaha, died suddenly.
The Buddha asked the king to leave her body in the charnel ground for some days and then offer it for sale. At first for a thousand coins. Then for less.

teach.h: SIRIMĀ: NO ONE WOULD TAKE IT.

teach.b: Verse one fifty calls the body a city: "After a stronghold has been made of the bones, it is covered with flesh and blood, and there dwell in it old age and death, pride and deceit."
A fortress built of bones, with some uninvited tenants. This is meant to loosen vanity, not to make anyone hate their body. The same tradition calls a human life rare and precious.
The point is to see clearly, and then use the time.

how: Some Buddhist monastics practice reflection on the body and on aging as a way to loosen attachment and vanity, and some lay Buddhists recite a short reflection that aging, sickness and death are natural to everyone.

o: a burning fire that cleanses what it touches
old age, the slow wearing-out of all things
the gift of being born a human being

games.q: match each image to where it comes from.
p: the fires of the fire sermon

s: the verse tells people never to laugh
it asks why we laugh while the world burns, and says: seek a light.
in the fire sermon, the fires include greed, hatred and delusion
these verses teach hatred of the body
they loosen vanity; the same tradition calls a human life rare and precious.

games.q: the beautiful Sirimā has died. the king offers her body for sale: a thousand coins, then less, then free. what happens?
o: no one will take it, even for nothing.
games.why: no one would take it. the commentary tells the story beside verse 147, as a picture of how beauty passes.

practice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and look at them: the lines, the knuckles, maybe a scar you remember getting.
These hands have carried groceries, held other hands, typed a thousand messages, and they're changing too, a little every day; look at them kindly, the way you'd look at an old friend's face.
Then close your eyes and feel them from the inside, the warmth, the tingling, the pulse: borrowed, not owned, and still good company.

wordCard.voice: Jara. Old age, decay: verse one forty-six asks why laughter, why joy, when the world is always burning, and says seek a light.

orig.note: Pali: old age, decay; chapter eleven is the Jarāvagga, the chapter on old age.

carryVoice: Your line: the world is on fire. The verse's answer is a light. That's one hundred eighty-seven days.
